Why are you interested in Duolingo?
entries.value: What draws me to Duolingo is that the product has to work for half a billion people who will quit if it stops being useful, which is a much harder constraint than a demo. Most of what I have built runs into that same wall. With ClarityAtlas, the iOS health app I lead technically at Open Health Intelligence, the interesting problem was not the model but whether someone would keep opening it. I built passive sleep estimation from HealthKit and Core Motion signals like step count, gait speed, and movement patterns specifically so users would not need a wearable, and we shipped it into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users. The underlying question I care about, how technology can increase a person's own judgment rather than quietly replacing it, is basically a learning question, and Duolingo is one of the few places working on it at real scale. I also like that decisions are made from evidence. My Intelehealth work, where I designed an evaluation framework comparing LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard, taught me that deciding whether an output should be trusted is usually harder than generating it. I would want to work on that side of the product.

entries.label: How will your personal experiences make an impact at Duolingo?
entries.value: Two habits I would bring. First, I own systems end to end rather than isolated pieces. At Summer Atlantic Capital I built the machine-learning core of an anomaly-detection system, including the repository and CI scaffold, the event-ingestion pipeline, a versioned FastAPI microservice, temporal sequence models over event streams, and a learning-to-rank layer for prioritizing alerts. The thing I kept returning to was operational usefulness: an anomaly system that fires too often creates a second problem instead of solving the first, so ranking and explanation quality mattered as much as raw detection performance. I expect that instinct to transfer to any system where output volume can outrun human attention. Second, I think carefully about where automation should stop. In a Playwright-based job-application agent I built in TypeScript, I made SQLite the single source of truth because browser automation gets dangerous when state diverges across processes, put every mutating capability behind fail-closed flags, and architecturally prevented free-text and demographic fields from being auto-filled. I also built a validation ladder so nothing counts as working just because it passed against a local fixture. I would rather ship something narrower and actually verified than something broad and unreliable.
